title: Shameful History: Project 100,000
summary: Josh and Chuck cover Project 100,000, the 1966–1971 US military program that lowered intelligence standards to enlist roughly 354,000 men, many with low IQs, mostly from poor and minority backgrounds, who were sent to fight in Vietnam. The episode traces its roots in World War II and Korean War manpower shortages, Daniel Patrick Moynihan's anti-poverty rationale, Kennedy and LBJ's support, Robert McNamara's earlier STEP program that Congress rejected, and the deferment loopholes that drove the need for infantry. They discuss the New Standards recruits' high casualty and psychiatric referral rates, recruiter fraud and ringers, dishonorable "bad paper" discharges, postwar hardship compared with other veterans, Bill Daniel's appeals, McNamara's lack of apology, and critics such as Joe Galloway. The episode closes with listener mail about unusual surnames and middle names.
topics: military recruitment standards World War II

segments.title: Opening and welcome
segments.summary: Hosts open the show and introduce the episode's topic.

segments.title: Origins of the episode and framing
segments.summary: The idea was suggested by listener David Bryant's mother. Hosts introduce Robert McNamara's role and the nickname McNamara's Morons, and preview the program as a wartime effort to lower military recruitment standards. Brief tangent about M*A*S*H.

segments.title: Manpower shortages in World War II
segments.summary: The military faced shortages of combat soldiers after specialists were assigned to technical roles, and chose to lower intelligence standards.
topics: military recruitment standards World War II

segments.title: WWII remedial education and return to higher standards
segments.summary: About 350,000 men were admitted between 1942 and 1945 under lowered standards, and the army provided remedial education. Standards were raised again after the war, and the Korean War brought the same shortage.

segments.title: Moynihan's anti-poverty rationale and political support
segments.summary: Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan argued that enlisting low-scoring men would lift them out of poverty. Kennedy and Johnson supported the idea, and early critics included military leaders.

segments.title: Kennedy and Johnson quotes
segments.summary: Hosts riff on quotes attributed to Kennedy and Johnson about recruits and the program.

segments.title: Early critics and the STEP program
segments.summary: Military leaders and others, such as Job Corps supporters, opposed the plan. McNamara proposed the Special Training Enlistment Program in 1964, which Congress refused to fund, and in 1966 he adopted a Marine-inspired special training approach military-wide.

segments.title: Draft deferments and US combat troops in Vietnam
segments.summary: Project 100,000 was officially announced in 1966 amid a manpower shortage caused by draft deferments, such as marriage, college, medical and conscientious objector, plus evasion through the National Guard, Coast Guard, or fleeing abroad. The US sent ground combat troops to South Vietnam in 1966 after the Gulf of Tonkin incident.

segments.title: Program duration and civil rights critics
segments.summary: The program ran from October 1, 1966 through 1971. Civil rights leaders, including Congressman Adam Clayton Powell, criticized it as genocide for poor Black Americans. Recruits were called New Standards men.

segments.title: Demographics and test scores of recruits
segments.summary: About 354,000 men were admitted, 91 percent below previous minimum IQ requirements, with an average AFQT score implying an IQ near 75. Forty-eight percent came from the South and 38 percent were non-white.

segments.title: Recruiter fraud and ringers
segments.summary: Recruiters made misleading promises and paid ringers to take qualification tests for illiterate recruits. Recruiters also used administrative acceptance to admit men who failed tests.

segments.title: Mistreatment in basic training
segments.summary: Recruits were bullied by drill sergeants and platoon members. Special training companies sometimes failed, and recruits were recycled or passed without meeting standards.

segments.title: Hamilton Gregory's accounts of unprepared recruits
segments.summary: Gregory described recruits who did not know their state or that the US was at war, posing danger to their platoons.

segments.title: Combat deployment and casualties
segments.summary: Around half or more were shipped to Vietnam and most reached front lines. 478 were killed, a fatality rate about three times the average, 1,300 died to mines and booby traps, about 20,000 were injured, and about 500 were amputees.

segments.title: Horror stories and AWOL and psychiatric referrals
segments.summary: Hosts recount a recruit named Jerry who accidentally killed an officer on night guard. New Standards men were referred for psychiatric evaluation ten times as often, with suicide attempts and attacks on soldiers leading to stockade and dishonorable discharges. Comparison to Full Metal Jacket.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break before the second half of the episode.

segments.title: Mike Sanchez's positive story
segments.summary: Mike Sanchez, a pseudonymous recruit, was protected by two commanding officers. He earned a Silver Star for rescuing a wounded officer and later served as a driver with a passenger-seat arrangement. He later became a barber. Jim Bracewell wrote about him.

segments.title: Elmer's sick bay story
segments.summary: A recruit named Elmer, reported by Dave Rus, excelled at keeping a Navy sick bay clean. Hosts note that recruits could have been placed in suitable roles rather than used as expendable front-line troops.

segments.title: Postwar outcomes and bad paper discharges
segments.summary: Project 100,000 veterans had higher PTSD rates, unemployment, homelessness, drug addiction, and suicide than other Vietnam veterans. A 1980s study found 10 percent of low-IQ veterans unemployed versus 3 percent of non-veterans. About half received discharges other than honorable, stigmatizing them and limiting VA help.

segments.title: Bill Daniel's discharge appeals
segments.summary: Veteran and former recruiter Bill Daniel appealed bad paper discharges and succeeded in about 400 cases out of roughly 180,000 dishonorable discharges. Recruits were mostly discharged for being unsuitable, a condition the military had selected them for.

segments.title: McNamara's legacy and critics' views
segments.summary: McNamara apologized for escalating Vietnam but never for Project 100,000. Hamilton Gregory believed he had good intentions. Joe Galloway, who wrote We Were Soldiers, criticized McNamara after his death, saying he was going to hell over the program. McNamara's memoir In Retrospect and The Fog of War are mentioned.

segments.title: Wrap-up of the topic
segments.summary: Hosts close the topic and credit David Bryant's mom for the suggestion.

segments.title: Listener mail: unusual surnames and middle names
segments.summary: A listener reports a customer with the surname Why, whose card required a second letter, and notes that she and her sister were not given middle names. Jane Trahanofski, owner of Levon's Florals in Newport Beach, is mentioned.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener emails and sign off.
